query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thermomechanical processing treatment—involving hot deformation at approximately 900°C followed by rapid quenching—to the as‐cast single-phase titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy will refine the grain structure and lock in a high density of beneficial microstructural features, thereby enhancing its yield strength, ductility, and creep resistance during elevated-temperature or extreme-environment mechanical testing compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase solid-solution titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical treatment consisting of hot deformation at ~900°C, immediately followed by rapid quenching
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated-temperature regimes (e.g., 600–1000°C) or extreme environmental conditions where mechanical performance (tensile, creep) is critical
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain size and preserved dislocation structures acquired via dynamic recrystallization during hot deformation, maintained by rapid quenching
generation.mechanism: Hot deformation at 900°C induces dynamic recrystallization, reducing grain size and generating a high density of grain boundaries and dislocation structures. The subsequent rapid quenching freezes these microstructural features in place, inhibiting grain coarsening and enhancing diffusion-controlled deformation resistance, which together improve strength and ductility at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, the treated material is expected to exhibit higher yield strength, improved ductility, and slower creep rates under elevated-temperature testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties of the untreated as-cast titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy
generation.boundary: This effect is applicable to Ti–Ni high-entropy alloys in a single-phase solid-solution state and is expected to be evident under high-temperature (600–1000°C) or extreme-environment mechanical tests; effects outside these regimes or in multiphase alloys are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism of grain refinement suggests improved mechanical properties, the exact magnitude of enhancements and their stability over extended testing durations remain uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy samples: one set undergoes the proposed TMP treatment (hot deformation at 900°C followed by rapid quenching) and the other is retained in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to controlled elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and creep testing at 800°C).
measurements: Grain size and microstructural features via SEM/EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, ductility, and creep resistance compared to the as-cast samples under the specified testing conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Performance of the Zr7 MEA after TMT Processing
cited_evidence.text: On the basis of physical metallurgy, two factors can affect the recrystallization rate of HEAs; one is the rapid annealing temperature, and the other is the accumulation of strain energy. A higher annealing temperature allows for a sample to complete its recrystallization earlier, and it also coarsens recrystallized grains at a faster rate. A greater accumulation of strain energy also provides more driving force for enhancing the nucleation and grain growth rate of recrystallization.
